cards.text: A psalm of David, for the choirmaster, and David is talking to the LORD about the king. And friend, this king isn't a little bit happy. He is EXULTING, arms up, the whole thing!

cards.question: The king is rejoicing big time. What is he rejoicing in?

cards.text: Turns out the king had a desire in his heart and a request on his lips. David tells the LORD how that went, and then comes a Selah.

cards.question: True or false: the LORD held back what the king asked for.

cards.text: And the LORD welcomes the king with rich blessings. Then He places something on the king's head, and I promise you it's fancier than my chef's hat.

cards.question: What does the LORD place on the king's head?

cards.text: Pure GOLD, friend. I went for twenty-five cents in a closing-sale bin, and this man is wearing a gold crown. Now hear what the king actually asked the LORD for.

cards.question: The king asked the LORD for ___.

cards.text: He asked for life, and the LORD granted it: "length of days, forever and ever." I hit snooze for five extra minutes and feel guilty all morning, and this king walks away with FOREVER, plus splendor and majesty!

cards.question: The LORD grants the king blessings forever. And the king's joy? It comes from being with the ___.

cards.text: That is a LOT of blessing for one king. Then David says what's underneath it all, and it starts with something the king does.

cards.question: Under all those blessings, what is the one thing the king does?
The king trusts in the LORD, and through the loving devotion of the Most High, he will not be ___.

cards.text: Then the psalm turns from gold crowns to enemies: "Your right hand will seize those who hate You." That's a faster mood change than a group chat right after somebody types, "We need to talk."
At the time of the appearing, the enemies are placed in a fiery furnace. In His wrath the LORD will engulf them, and the fire will consume them.

cards.question: True or false: the descendants of those enemies will live on among the sons of men.
True or false: the enemies plan harm, but the schemes they come up with won't succeed.
Picture a bow trained right on those enemies. What happens to them?

cards.text: Last line, and suddenly it's not just David talking. The psalm says "we." It calls out, "Be exalted, O LORD, in Your strength" and then the people make Him a promise.

cards.question: In the psalm's last line, what do the people say they will do?

findings.problem: David appears for the first time here and is never introduced. The card just says "A psalm of David" and "David is talking to the LORD" without saying simply who he is. That can be done without saying he is the king in this psalm.

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: Psalm 21:6 says "You cheer him with joy in Your presence." The question says the king's joy "comes from being with the ___," which makes the LORD's presence the cause of the joy. The text says the LORD cheers him with joy in His presence and leaves that link open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question calls trusting in the LORD "the one thing the king does." In the passage the king also rejoices and exults (21:1) and asks the LORD for life (21:4), so "the one thing" isn't true.

rule.text: What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: The fill in the blank repeats Psalm 21:7 almost word for word and asks the baker to supply the line's last word ("shaken"). That is guessing the next words of a line, not a question about movement or meaning. The wrong answers don't really compete either. "Crowned" is already ruled out by card 6, and "honored" goes against everything the earlier cards told, so the card is won by elimination rather than reasoning.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The card is close to a bare restatement of 21:9 with none of Papa Dorin's voice. "At the time of the appearing" drops "Your" from the text and leaves the baker with no idea whose appearing it is, so the moment doesn't make sense on its own.

rule.text: A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The card says the people "make Him a promise." Psalm 21:13 says "we will sing and praise Your power" and never calls it a promise.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: "Suddenly it's not just David talking" and "the people" (also in card 20's question) say who the "we" in 21:13 is and that the speaker changes. The text only says "we" and leaves the speakers open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The joke compares the psalm's own turn, from blessing to judgment, to a group chat after "We need to talk." It lands right before the fiery furnace and wrath of 21:9. The joke's target is the structure of Scripture itself rather than a person's human situation, and the reverence rule doesn't say clearly whether that is allowed.
findings.question: Does joking about how a passage itself is written, like its sudden mood change, count as humor that "targets Scripture," especially going into a passage about God's judgment?
